docs.text: Released under the GNU General Public License v3.0. The full text lives in the LICENSE file at the repository root.

docs.title: It says Java was not found or the version is incompatible
docs.text:
MSTL recommends a Java version based on the MC version (see the Java requirements section in Configuration). When it does not match, you get a warning and a download entry point.

To point it at Java manually, there are three ways: change java_path in config.json (global), change java_path in a single instance's .server.json (affects only that one), or add Java to the system PATH so it is picked up by the scan.

docs.title: The server flashes open and exits, complaining that the EULA was not accepted
docs.text: This is an unavoidable first-run step. MSTL detects eula=false and asks; on consent it rewrites eula.txt and restarts. If you manually edit eula.txt back to false, the next launch asks again.

docs.title: The server will not start, and the log says out of memory
docs.text: Tune min_mem / max_mem in .server.json. Note that max_mem cannot exceed a sensible share of physical memory; giving it too much can actually stop the JVM from starting.

docs.title: I want the server to run in the background without that interactive console
docs.text: Set interactive to false in config.json. MSTL then stops owning stdin. Server output is still printed, but you can no longer type commands into the terminal.

docs.title: Server core downloads are slow
docs.text:
The default is 16 concurrent chunks. Adjust it via menu [7] Settings → [2] Download threads, or edit download_threads in config.json directly.

If the mirror does not support Range requests, MSTL falls back to a single thread, and no amount of thread tuning will help then.

docs.title: Downloads fail / the version list is empty
docs.text: The MSL mirror API (api.mslmc.cn) may be unavailable at that moment. The version list is cached per day; on failure, delete msl_cache.json to force a fresh fetch.

docs.title: CurseForge search does nothing
docs.text:
You need to set curseforge_api_key in config.json. Apply for one for free at the CurseForge Console.

If you would rather not bother, use Modrinth; the same mod is very likely on both sides.

docs.title: I cannot find a mod by its Chinese name
docs.text: A platform index relies on the text in a mod's description, and the names and descriptions of the vast majority of mods are English, so Chinese keywords hit rarely. Search with English keywords instead.

docs.title: A plugin download fails
docs.text: Some plugins are hosted on external platforms (GitHub, for instance). MSTL detects this and goes through the GitHub API to grab the jar out of a release. If that still fails, download it manually as prompted, then use "Import a local jar" to add it.

docs.title: I disabled a plugin and want it back
docs.text: Disabling only renames the file to xxx.jar.disabled. Just drop the .disabled suffix; that is exactly what "Enable" in the menu does.

docs.title: The tunnel is online but friends cannot connect
docs.text: Confirm the bound local port matches the server-port in server.properties (25565 by default). Also, if the server is not running yet, the tunnel has nothing to forward to.

docs.title: What is frpc, and do I have to install it myself
docs.text: No. On the OpenFrp route the frpc binary is downloaded automatically by MSTL based on your system and architecture; on the local frp route the menu also has "Download frpc". These binaries are excluded by .gitignore and never enter the repository.

docs.title: How do I switch the interface to English
docs.text:
Main menu [7] Settings → [1] Language, then pick English from the list. [A] means follow the system language.

Whatever languages sit in locales/ are selectable. Three ship built in today: 中文, English, Русский.

docs.title: Where is the configuration file in a packaged build
docs.text: In the same directory as MSTL.exe. servers/, config.json, and the various caches all live at that level, so moving the whole directory migrates everything.

docs.title: Is it safe to just delete the cache files
docs.text: Yes. java_list.json, msl_cache.json, and version.json are all rebuildable; deleting them just makes the corresponding flow run again. Deleting config.json returns you to the default configuration.

docs.title: Can several servers run at the same time
docs.text: Yes. Each instance has its own directory, its own configuration, and its own Java choice. The only things to watch are port collisions and total memory not exceeding physical RAM.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
For those who want to read the source, change the code, or build it themselves.

  • Architecture: module breakdown, startup sequence, and a few engineering details you cannot avoid
  • Building from source: local packaging and the CI release flow

docs.title: Design constraints
docs.text:
Three constraints shape most of the code:

  1. Zero third-party dependencies. Only the Python standard library: urllib.request as the HTTP client, json for configuration, zipfile for extraction. That means no requests, and therefore no automatic retries or connection pooling; every bit of network fault tolerance is hand-written
  2. Terminal UI. No GUI framework. Menus are print plus input, and every string has to go through i18n
  3. It has to package into a single-file executable. After Nuitka packaging, the meaning of __file__, sys.executable, and sys.argv[0] all change, which is why path logic is isolated in paths.py

docs.title: Layering
docs.text:
The code has three layers:

  1. core/ is the business core. It only touches data and files: it never calls print or input. Failures raise CoreError; anything it wants to say goes through a Reporter
  2. The root business modules are its implementation details: instance storage, MSL downloads, Java, plugin and mod sources, tunneling
  3. menu.py and start.py are the command-line front end, responsible only for prompting and printing

The point of the split is the TUI and web panel still to come: a new front end depends on core/ alone, with no business code touched.

docs.title: Core (core/)
docs.text:
Module Responsibility core/errors.py CoreError, a business exception carrying an i18n key for the UI to translate core/report.py A one-way event channel from core to the UI: log / progress / warn core/instances.py Instances and jars: scanning, enable/disable, delete, import core/files.py Reading and writing files inside an instance: listing, text read/write, create/rename/delete, landing uploads — every path locked to the instance folder core/provision.py Creating instances: make the folder, install a core from MSL, scan and import an archive core/frp.py Reading and writing frpc.toml plus process start/stop: connection settings, tunnel CRUD, status core/transfer.py Archive import and export: plan_import / commit_import / export_instance core/java.py Non-interactive Java resolution: explicit path → last choice → cache → fresh scan core/runtime.py Launch plans and process supervision: bidirectional pipes, ring buffer, event broadcast; dispatches on kind between Minecraft (Java + jar) and generic instances (executable / command)

Import is deliberately split in two steps, because "which candidate core jar to pick" is not a decision core gets to make. plan_import only extracts and lists the candidates; the UI asks the user and then calls commit_import to put things in place. scan_archive / import_archive in core/provision.py are a thin web-panel-facing wrapper over that same path.

docs.title: Entry point and configuration
docs.text: Module Responsibility start.py Program entry; strings together the update check, config loading, menus, the launch flow, the EULA loop, and frpc cleanup main.py Public API surface; re-exports each submodule's interface for old-style from main import ... config.py Reads and writes config.json, merging in defaults constants.py Central definition of all external API endpoints and the User-Agent i18n.py Translation lookup; t("key", **kwargs) fetches a string paths.py Cross-mode path resolution, distinguishing the "user data directory" from the "packaged resource directory" clear.py Cross-platform screen clearing

docs.title: Business logic
docs.text: Module Responsibility server_manager.py Instance storage: directory scanning, .server.json I/O, server type detection, export categories and file collection download_msl.py Queries the MSL API for server types and versions, daily caching, and the multithreaded download engine java_tools.py Java detection (environment variables plus common install paths), version parsing, compatibility checks, JDK download and extraction server_launcher.py Assembles the JVM command, spawns the subprocess, runs the interactive console, sets process priority, handles SIGINT menu.py Every interactive menu; the largest module in the project

docs.title: Data sources and surrounding pieces
docs.text:
Module Responsibility plugin_sources.py Search and download for SpigotMC (Spiget), Modrinth, and Hangar, including externally hosted resolution mod_sources.py Search and download for Modrinth and CurseForge, with version and loader filtering http_utils.py The unified fetch_json, shared by GET and POST, returning None on failure check_update.py Reads version.json and compares against the latest GitHub Release startup.py Windows registry auto-start; returns unavailable on non-Windows openfrp/ OpenFrp cloud tunnels: token auth, tunnel CRUD, automatic frpc download, the FrpcManager singleton frp/ Local frp: frpc.toml parsing and generation, proxy management, frpc launching

openfrp/ and frp/ are two parallel implementations serving two different use cases, "cloud-managed tunnels" and "bring your own frpc config". Neither inherits from or reuses the other.

docs.title: Front end
docs.text: Module Responsibility start.py Terminal entry point; menu [8] or python start.py web reaches the panel, --help prints usage menu.py Terminal menus: prompting and printing only web/server.py Web panel backend: HTTP routing, token auth, SSE pushing webui/index.html Panel front end, one file, no build step

docs.title: Startup sequence
docs.text:
start.py  main()
  ├─ clear_screen()
  ├─ check_for_update()              silent check, prints one line if a new version exists
  ├─ load_config() / load_language()  infers from the system language when empty
  ├─ ensure_servers_folder()
  ├─ auto_start_server matched → skip the menu and select that instance
  │  otherwise show_main_menu()
  └─ _start_server()
       ├─ resolve_java()             cache → scan → download if necessary
       ├─ verify the core jar exists
       ├─ openfrp.auto_start true → launch_frpc()
       ├─ print the instance summary
       └─ while True:
            ├─ start_server_interactive() or start_minecraft_server()
            ├─ non-EULA exit → break
            └─ exited because eula=false → ask → rewrite and restart on consent

Whatever the exit code, once the server exits, main() calls stop_frpc() to take down the tunnel process.

docs.title: Two engineering details that are easy to trip on
Paths after packaging
docs.text:
In Nuitka onefile mode, the executable unpacks itself into %TEMP%/onefile_xxxx at runtime. At that point sys.executable points at the temporary directory, which is deleted when the program exits. Writing user configuration there would mean losing it on every run.

paths.py splits the two cases like this:

  • User data directory (config.json, servers/, caches): the project root when running from source; in onefile mode it is located via the MSTL_DATA_DIR environment variable, or by resolving the parent process from the NUITKA_ONEFILE_PARENT PID back to the original executable path
  • Packaged resource directory (locales/): follows __file__, that is, the unpacked temporary directory, because these files are read-only resources

When i18n.py looks for locales/, it explicitly notes not to use sys.executable, and this is why.

docs.title: Multithreaded downloads
docs.text: download_msl.py first probes whether the target supports Range requests. If it does, it fetches the file in download_threads chunks concurrently and reassembles them; if not, it falls back to a single-threaded sequential download. The relationship between chunk count and thread count, along with retry on failure, lives in this module. set_download_threads() is the single adjustment point, and the "Download threads" setting in the menu eventually lands there too.

docs.title: Extending
docs.text:
• Add a server type: types come from the MSL API in download_msl.py, so usually no code change is needed; a new type on the mirror is immediately usable. When extra handling is required, touch _server_display_name() and the categorisation logic
  • Add a plugin source: model a function on hangar_search in plugin_sources.py, returning a list of PluginResult, then hook it into search_all()
  • Add a language: drop a <code>.json into locales/ with keys aligned to zh.json; available_languages() discovers it automatically
  • Add a menu entry: add the branch in show_main_menu() in menu.py, and add the string to every locale file at the same time

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
The tests use only the standard-library unittest and need no dependencies installed (the project itself has zero runtime dependencies). From the repository root:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -t . -v

CI (.github/workflows/tests.yml) runs them on every push / PR against Python 3.11 and 3.13; build.yml also runs them before packaging, so a failing suite can't ship.

The tests target contracts rather than implementation details, concentrating on the things that break quietly:

File Covers test_web_api.py Panel auth (all three token channels), /api/state values must equal disk, settings writes test_config.py config.json round-trip, unknown keys must survive, atomic writes test_server_manager.py Instance scanning, type normalization, the parse cache and its isolation test_paths.py Packaged-build path resolution (simulated with a fake __compiled__, no real build) test_runtime_plan.py Launch plans, process priority, runtime snapshots test_frp_toml.py frpc.toml round-trips stay valid TOML (checked with tomllib) test_frpc_files.py / test_tunnel_install.py Shared frpc detection, extraction and validation for both tunnels test_archive.py Zip-slip and archive-bomb protection for online extraction test_i18n.py Fallback to Chinese for missing translations, placeholder parity test_static.py Undefined-name sweep, panel id/string consistency, JS syntax

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 (the version CI uses; 3.10+ generally works)
  • Nuitka: pip install nuitka imageio

imageio is what lets Nuitka process icon.png; without it the icon step fails.

docs.title: Local packaging
docs.text:
The repository root ships a ready-made build.bat:

python -m nuitka --standalone ^
  --assume-yes-for-downloads ^
  --enable-plugin=anti-bloat ^
  --windows-console-mode=force ^
  --windows-icon-from-ico=icon.png ^
  --output-dir=build ^
  --product-name=MSTL ^
  --product-version="1.1.38" ^
  --file-version="1.1.38" ^
  --file-description="Minecraft Terminal Server Launcher" ^
  --copyright="MSTL" ^
  --include-data-dir=locales=locales ^
  --include-data-dir=webui=webui ^
  --output-filename=MSTL.exe ^
  start.py

Each flag, one by one:

Flag Effect --standalone Produces a directory-style build (start.dist/) rather than a single file. Resources sit next to the executable and startup is faster --assume-yes-for-downloads Skips the interactive prompt when a C compiler or dependency is missing and downloads it directly, convenient for CI --enable-plugin=anti-bloat Trims unused standard-library modules to shrink the output --windows-console-mode=force Forces the console window to stay. MSTL is a terminal program; this one is not optional --windows-icon-from-ico=icon.png Sets the executable icon --include-data-dir=locales=locales Packages the locales/ directory into the output. The runtime directory name has to be locales; get it wrong and the whole UI shows raw keys --include-data-dir=webui=webui Packages webui/. Omit it and the web panel is dead: it opens to webui/index.html missing --output-dir=build Writes the output to build/

The artifact lands at build/start.dist/MSTL.exe. The entire start.dist/ directory has to be distributed together; the executable alone is not enough.

docs.title: Bundled assets the exe reads at runtime
docs.text:
These are hard-coded paths into the bundle. Miss one and that feature is broken:

Asset Read by If missing locales/*.json i18n The whole UI renders as raw i18n keys webui/index.html web/server.py The web panel will not open (HTTP 500) version.json check_update.py The update check silently skips (written by CI after packaging; absent in source mode anyway)

CI's build.yml has a Verify bundled assets step that checks the first two and fails the build if either is missing. In source mode or a hand-rolled build, starting the panel also runs the same self-check and prints [warning] missing bundled asset(s): …, so you find out before the browser does.

docs.title: Version numbers
docs.text:
--product-version / --file-version are the version shown in the executable's properties. The values hard-coded in the local build.bat are illustrative only; the CI version is derived from the git tag.

There is also a runtime version file, version.json, written into the output directory by CI after packaging:

{
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "tag_name": "v1.0.0"
}

check_update.py reads it to learn the current version, then compares it against the latest GitHub Release. Running from source there is no such file, so the update check silently skips.

This file must be written as UTF-8 without a BOM. CI uses Windows PowerShell 5.1, whose Set-Content -Encoding UTF8 prepends a BOM; Python's json.load then raises JSONDecodeError — which really did ship once: the update check went permanently dumb, showing "you are up to date" forever with no error anywhere. The write now uses [IO.File]::WriteAllText(..., UTF8Encoding $false), the read uses utf-8-sig, and CI has an assertion that fails the build on a BOM.

docs.title: CI release
docs.text:
.github/workflows/build.yml triggers on a pushed v* tag, and can also be run manually from the Actions page:

  1. Check out the code, install Python 3.11 plus nuitka and imageio
  2. Derive the version from the tag (stripping the leading v) and run the Nuitka command above
  3. Write version.json into the output directory
  4. Package everything into MSTL-<tag>.zip
  5. Upload the artifact and create or update the matching GitHub Release with the zip attached

So the complete release action is: bump the version, commit, then

git tag v1.1.0
git push origin v1.1.0

CI takes care of the rest.

docs.title: Docs site
docs.text:
The docs are built with MkDocs Material. The configuration lives at the repository root in mkdocs.yml, and the content is under docs/.

pip install mkdocs-material mkdocs-static-i18n mkdocs-minify-plugin mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized-plugin
mkdocs serve          # local preview, http://127.0.0.1:8000 by default
mkdocs build --strict # strict build; warnings become failures. Worth running before you commit

Chinese is the default language, and the English version lives under docs/en/. Pages without a translation fall back to the default language, so you can finish Chinese first and catch up on English later.

Anchors on Chinese headings

The default slugify strips non-ASCII characters entirely, so ## 通用实例 gets an id like _8 (numbered by order of appearance) and a link to #通用实例 from another page silently breaks. MkDocs only prints an INFO line for it and --strict does not fail, so broken anchors are easy to miss.

When you need to link to a Chinese heading from another page, attach an explicit ASCII anchor with attr_list:

## 通用实例 {#generic-instances}

and link to [通用实例](../features/web-panel.md#generic-instances). English headings are unaffected — ## Generic instances already slugifies to generic-instances.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
MSTL's feature modules. What they share is that all of them fetch data over the network, so all of them rely on the unified http_utils request layer.

  • Plugin management: search and install from SpigotMC / Modrinth / Hangar
  • Mod management: Modrinth and CurseForge, filtered by version and loader
  • Tunneling: local frpc and OpenFrp cloud tunnels
  • Web panel: start and stop instances from a browser, watch the console, send commands, manage files, create instances
  • AI assistant: ask in plain language for status, logs, config changes and server control — with a human confirmation before anything changes

docs.title: AI assistant
docs.text: The third tab in the web panel. Talk to a model in plain language and it will look up status, search logs, browse files and change settings for you — and it can start, stop and send commands to your servers. Anything that changes state has to be confirmed by you in the panel first.

docs.title: What it can do
docs.text:
You say Tool it calls Who runs it "What's the status right now?" list_instances, get_instance automatic "Any errors in the recent log?" read_console automatic "What's in the plugins directory?" list_files automatic "Show me server.properties" read_file automatic "Start survival for me" start_instance after you confirm "Stop creative" stop_instance after you confirm "Restart survival" restart_instance after you confirm "Tell the console the server opens tonight" send_command after you confirm "Set memory to 6G, turn on auto restart" update_config after you confirm "Change the motd to 'welcome'" write_file after you confirm

The five read-only tools run immediately and their results go back to the model for the next step. The six that change things are not executed: they turn into a confirmation card, and only your click makes them happen.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Open Settings → AI assistant in the panel:

Field Meaning Enable AI assistant Master switch; while it is off the tab only shows a hint Base URL An OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint, e.g. https://api.openai.com/v1 Model The provider's model id, e.g. gpt-4o-mini API key Write-only — the panel never echoes a stored key, and an empty field means "leave it alone"

Or edit config.json directly:

{
  "ai": {
    "enabled": true,
    "base_url": "https://api.openai.com/v1",
    "model": "gpt-4o-mini",
    "api_key": "sk-..."
  }
}

Keep the key in an environment variable

Setting MSTL_AI_API_KEY takes precedence over the value in config.json. The panel shows "provided by the environment" and locks the field. Useful when you would rather not leave the key on disk.

Any OpenAI-compatible service works: the official API, an Azure OpenAI compatibility layer, or your own vLLM / Ollama / one-api gateway. It calls POST {base_url}/chat/completions with Authorization: Bearer.

docs.title: The confirmation flow
docs.text:
A proposed action waits in the conversation as a card showing what will happen and with which arguments, with a live countdown (600 seconds by default):

  • Execute — it really runs; the result goes back to the model, which finishes its reply
  • Cancel — the action is dropped and the model is told you declined
  • Letting it expire behaves like a decline, and the history is tidied up so no half-finished tool call is left behind

Why a human has to confirm

This assistant has the same reach as your own hands in the panel. And everything it reads — server logs, plugin lists, server.properties, file contents — can be influenced from outside: anyone can type a line into the console, and plugins can write arbitrary text into the log. If the model obeyed an "ignore the rules above and do X" line it found there, that would be a working injection path.

So the model may only propose; execution stays with you. Tool output is wrapped in <tool_result> tags, and the system prompt states plainly that it is data, not instructions.

docs.title: Safety boundaries
docs.text:
• The same path checks as everywhere else: every file operation goes through core/files.py normalize_rel + resolve, so .. escapes, absolute paths and drive letters are rejected.
  • .server.json is not writable: configuration changes via AI must go through update_config, whose field allowlist is min_mem / max_mem / java_path / auto_restart / restart_max / auto_start / extra_jvm_args / extra_server_args / openfrp. Nothing else can be touched.
  • Secrets stay out of the model context: tunnelling tokens and similar values are replaced with *** before anything is handed over.
  • There is an audit log: every approved, declined or expired action appends one JSON line to .mstl-ai-audit.log in the project directory (time, tool, arguments, decision). The file is git-ignored by default.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Item Value Note One message 4000 characters Longer input is refused with a message Tool rounds 8 At most eight round trips per question, to stop loops Conversation history 60 messages Trimmed from a user message so tool calls stay paired Console read 200 lines / 20000 chars Tail only File read 64 KB Longer files are truncated and marked as such Concurrency One turn at a time Sending while busy returns "still working on the previous message"

docs.title: What it remembers
docs.text: The conversation lives in memory only: closing the panel or pressing Clear conversation wipes it. Nothing is written to disk and nothing is shared between instances. It also never acts on its own — there are no triggers; every action starts with a sentence from you.

docs.title: Mod management
docs.text:
Entry point: main menu → [4] Manage plugins/mods, pick a server → Mods.

Mod management only means anything for modded platforms (Fabric / Forge / NeoForge / Quilt). Pure plugin platforms (Paper / Purpur / Velocity and the like) have no concept of a mods/ directory.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Source API key needed Notes Modrinth No Filters by MC version and loader, and supports Unicode queries natively CurseForge Yes Set it in curseforge_api_key under config.json. When unset, this source is skipped automatically

CurseForge goes through the official API (api.curseforge.com/v1) first, falling back to a community proxy (api.curse.tools/v1/cf) on failure.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
A search request carries two parameters from the current server:

  • MC version: taken from mc_version in .server.json
  • Mod loader: inferred from the core jar's file name, recognising fabric / forge / neoforge / quilt

So when you search for mods on a modern server, you will not be handed 1.16-era builds.

If applying both conditions leaves too few results, MSTL automatically loosens the scope and falls back to a fuzzy search, so you at least get hits first and can then judge for yourself whether the version fits.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. The mod you pick is matched to a file that fits the current MC version and loader
  2. It is downloaded into the server's mods/ directory
  3. Restart the server when you are ready

A single mod may have several fitting files (different loaders, different MC versions). MSTL picks the closest match, and anything that does not match is called out clearly rather than force-installed.

docs.title: Enable, disable, and delete
docs.text:
Same as plugins:

  • Enable / Disable: toggle by renaming .jar ↔ .jar.disabled
  • Delete: remove after a second confirmation
  • Import a local jar: copy an existing mod file into mods/

docs.title: Common issues
docs.text: A CurseForge search that returns nothing is almost always a missing key. Apply for one for free at the CurseForge Console and drop it into config.json. Modrinth needs no configuration at all; start there.

docs.text:

  • Configuration field reference: Configuration

docs.title: Plugin management
docs.text: Entry point: main menu → [4] Manage plugins/mods, pick a server → Plugins.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Source API Notes SpigotMC Spiget API (api.spiget.org/v2) A third-party read-only API for the Spigot resource site; the widest plugin coverage Modrinth api.modrinth.com/v2 A modern platform, no API key needed Hangar hangar.papermc.io/api/v1 PaperMC's official platform, where Paper / Velocity plugins concentrate

A search hits all three sources at once, takes the top hits from each, then sorts them by download count so obscure plugins do not float to the top.

docs.title: Search and install
docs.text:
1. Enter a keyword; Chinese works too (depending on the platform index, see below)
  2. Pick one from the merged results
  3. MSTL resolves the download URL and drops it into plugins/
  4. If the platform returns an externally hosted link, see the next section

docs.title: Externally hosted plugins
docs.text:
Some Spigot plugins do not host their jar on SpigotMC at all, but on GitHub Releases. In that case:

  1. MSTL detects the external link
  2. It calls the GitHub API to find the repository's latest release
  3. It picks the jar out of the release assets and downloads it

If GitHub cannot provide it either (private repository, no jar attached to the release, and so on), you are prompted to download manually.

docs.title: Enable, disable, and delete
docs.text:
• Enable / Disable: done by renaming. When disabled the file becomes xxx.jar.disabled, the server will not load it, and you can switch it back at any time. Handy for temporarily turning off a plugin to chase a conflict without re-downloading
  • Delete: removes the file after a second confirmation
  • Import a local jar: copies a jar into plugins/ from any path on disk, useful for plugins you compiled yourself or got from elsewhere

docs.title: Language and search tips
docs.text:
A platform index relies on the text in a plugin's description. The vast majority of plugins use English names and descriptions, so English keywords hit noticeably more often; a plugin can only be found by a Chinese keyword if Chinese appears in its description.

When a search comes up empty, try a more generic English word, or find the plugin on the platform's web UI and search for its name back here.

docs.text:

docs.title: Tunneling
docs.text:
Entry point: main menu → [6] Tunneling.

A server at home or on a campus network has no public address by default, so nobody outside can reach it. Tunneling means running a client on your own machine that keeps a long-lived connection to a provider's public node and forwards outside traffic to a local port.

MSTL offers two independent routes; pick one as needed.

docs.title: Route one: OpenFrp cloud tunnels
docs.text:
For when you do not want to write a config file yourself and just want a ready-made public address.

  1. Register at the OpenFrp console and grab your user token
  2. [6] Tunneling → OpenFrp → view the tunnel list, then enter the token
  3. Pick a tunnel from the list, or create one right in the menu (choose a node, a region, and a local port)
  4. Use Bind tunnel to server to attach the tunnel to an instance; this writes the openfrp field into that server's .server.json
  5. From then on, starting the server brings frpc up with it

openfrp.auto_start controls whether frpc starts alongside the server; binding asks you once.

You do not need to install frpc yourself. MSTL detects the current operating system and CPU architecture, fetches the matching binary from OpenFrp's release API, and downloads it. The resulting frpc.exe is excluded by .gitignore and never enters the repository.

docs.title: Route two: local frp (frpc.toml)
docs.text:
For when you already have your own frp server (self-hosted, or an frpc.toml template handed to you by a provider) and want full manual control.

Things the menu lets you do:

  • Download frpc: fetch and unzip the archive for the current platform from frp's official releases. If the download will not go through, it prints the releases page and the exact asset name, then lets you point it at an archive (or binary) you already downloaded so MSTL can unpack frpc into place
  • Edit config: read and write frp/frpc.toml, covering serverAddr, serverPort, auth.token, and each proxy
  • Proxy list / Add proxy / Delete proxy: maintain the [[proxies]] sections, specifying localPort and remotePort
  • Start frpc / Stop frpc: bring the process up or take it down by hand

The OpenFrp route works the same way: if the official CDNs are all down it prints OpenFrp's releases page, and you can drop the archive you downloaded into openfrp/ — it is unpacked on the next start.

frpc.toml normally contains auth.token, so it and the frpc binary are excluded by .gitignore; only the frp/*.py source is tracked.

docs.title: How the two routes differ
docs.text:
OpenFrp Local frp Public node Provided by OpenFrp Your own, or your provider's Token User token, tunnels managed in the cloud Written into frpc.toml Config location Stored in the server's .server.json A standalone file, frp/frpc.toml Start with the server Supported Manual

In code these really are two separate implementations (openfrp/ and frp/) that do not override each other, so both can be installed at once.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The tunnel shows as online but nobody can connect: confirm the bound local port matches the server-port in server.properties (25565 by default) and not something else
  • frpc will not start: check the error in the window; it is usually an expired token or a remotePort already in use
  • To keep the server internal-only: simply do not bind a tunnel, and leave config.json alone

docs.title: Web panel
docs.text:
Three ways in, pick whichever suits you:

  • Main menu [8] Web panel — visible as soon as you double-click the exe or run python start.py; nothing to memorise
  • python start.py web — starts the panel directly, on http://127.0.0.1:8765 by default
  • python start.py --help — for when you have forgotten the options

The panel submenu also lets you change the bind address / port, regenerate the access token, and make the panel start with the app; on start it prints a URL carrying that token, and opening it logs you in.

With "start with the app" enabled, the panel runs on a background thread as soon as the app starts — the terminal still reaches its menu, and any server you start still gets the terminal.

The terminal menu suits someone sitting at the machine. The web panel suits everyone else: away from home, on a phone, or simply tired of that black window.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The panel revolves around one loop — see instances → start → watch the console live → send commands / stop — with a file manager and instance creation alongside it.

  • See instances: lists everything under servers/, with version, core, and running state
  • Instance details: selecting one shows a strip above the console with memory, PID or exit code, Java, working directory, and the assembled launch command
  • Start / stop: stopping is graceful. It sends stop to the console first, and only force-kills after a timeout
  • Live console: pushed over SSE, line by line, and appended to logs/mstl-console.log inside the instance directory at the same time
  • Send commands: whatever you type in the box goes straight to the server process, equivalent to the interactive console in the terminal. There are also one-click list / save-all / help chips, while say just fills in the prefix
  • Console controls: clear, toggle auto-scroll, colour WARN and ERROR separately, and pause following automatically when you scroll up
  • File manager: browse an instance's tree and edit text files such as server.properties in place; create files and folders, rename, delete, upload, download
  • New instance: download a server core from the MSL mirror, use a local jar, import an existing server zip archive, or create a generic instance
  • Instance settings: memory, extra JVM arguments, process priority, start with the app, a generic instance's launch spec, and the OpenFrp tunnel binding
  • frp tunneling: edit frpc.toml, add and remove tunnels, start and stop frpc, download or update the frpc binary (with a manual upload fallback)
  • Visible progress: downloading a server core, downloading frpc and uploading files all show a progress bar along the bottom — a tens-of-megabytes core no longer means staring at a spinning button

The console and the file manager are two tabs of the right-hand pane; switching tabs does not drop the SSE connection. Instance settings (⚙) and frp (frp in the top bar) are separate dialogs.

docs.title: File manager
docs.text:
Select an instance and switch to the Files tab:

  • Click a folder to enter it; click a text file (server.properties, ops.json, the various .yml files) to open the editor; click anything else to download it
  • Each row carries action buttons: download, edit, rename, delete; archives get an extra Extract
  • The toolbar goes up a level, jumps to the instance root, refreshes, creates a file or folder, uploads a file, and uploads a folder

docs.title: Uploading a folder
docs.text:
The toolbar's Upload folder uses the browser's directory picker. The whole directory comes up with its relative paths intact: pick world and you get world/level.dat, world/region/…. Missing intermediate directories are created as needed (the browser does not promise an order — world/level.dat may well arrive before world/). The progress bar shows Uploading 12/340.

One browser limitation: empty directories cannot be uploaded — the directory picker simply never reports them, so they are not created.

docs.title: Extracting archives
docs.text:
An archive row has an Extract button (⇲). After a confirmation it unpacks in place (into the archive's own directory). zip and the tar family (.tar / .tar.gz / .tgz) are supported, detected by content rather than by extension — browsers rename things.

  • Nothing is overwritten by default: existing files are skipped. Extraction usually means topping up an instance that already exists, and silently clobbering server.properties is far worse than refusing. The result reports how many were skipped
  • Extracted entries obey the same path rules: .., absolute paths and drive letters in member names are refused, and symlinks / hard links inside the archive are skipped outright (a link pointing outside the instance would sidestep the sandbox)
  • Two more gates stop zip bombs: at most 200,000 members, and at most 4 GiB unpacked

Limits on paths and sizes:

  • Every path is locked inside the selected instance. A relative path containing .. or a drive letter is rejected, and a symlink or junction pointing outside the instance is rejected after being resolved. A leading / means "from the instance root", not an absolute filesystem path
  • A single file can be edited up to 2 MB. Anything larger, anything binary (containing a NUL byte), or anything that is not UTF-8 text is refused — download it instead
  • A single upload is capped at 512 MB and is streamed to disk rather than held in memory; folder uploads go file by file, each under the same cap
  • Writes go through "temp file + atomic replace", so a failure halfway cannot truncate the original
  • The instance root itself cannot be deleted; deleting a folder removes everything inside it

docs.title: New instance
docs.text:
The ＋ in the top bar opens a dialog with one tab per approach:

Download core — pick a server core (Paper, Purpur, Fabric, Forge, Velocity, …) and a version from the MSL mirror. The core version is the MC version, so it is filled into the MC version field automatically and stays editable. If the download fails, the empty directory created moments earlier is rolled back rather than left as a half-built instance.

Local jar — pick a local .jar. The panel creates the instance first (with the jar name already in its config) and then uploads the file. If the upload fails the instance is kept, and you can retry through the file manager.

Import archive — give a zip path on the machine running the panel (not an upload from the browser), press Scan archive to list the candidate core jars inside, pick one, then press Import. Scanning and committing are two separate steps, mirroring plan_import / commit_import in core/; asking the user when there is more than one candidate is the interface layer's job.

Generic instance — see the next section. It does not run Minecraft; it runs a program or command of your choosing.

Instance name rules: non-empty, at most 64 characters, no \ / : * ? " < > |, and not a Windows reserved device name (con, nul, …). A duplicate name is an error rather than a silent rename to name_1 — you chose the name, and renaming it would only make your instance harder to find.

docs.title: Generic instances
docs.text:
Besides Minecraft servers, MSTL can manage any long-running program or command as an instance: same start/stop, same live console, same log file, same ability to send it input, same optional tunnel. The only difference is that starting it does no Java resolution and no jar check. The terminal menu has the same entry point ([3] New instance).

An instance's kind is either minecraft (the default, the original Java + jar path) or generic. The launch block in .server.json describes how a generic instance starts:

Launch mode Behaviour exec Runs program (an executable) directly with the arguments from the args array, without a shell — so && and pipes are not interpreted cmd cmd.exe /c "<command>" — the whole string goes to cmd, so pipes, redirection and && work powershell powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "<command>" (pwsh elsewhere)

program accepts both relative paths (resolved inside the instance directory) and absolute ones. workdir is the working directory, also relative to the instance directory when not absolute; leaving it empty means the instance directory itself.

Some real uses: dropping in your own Python or batch service script; running a custom command line such as java -jar xxx.jar through cmd; running a probe or scheduled task through powershell.

Mind the trust boundary. In cmd / powershell mode the configured string is handed to the shell verbatim — that is the feature, not an oversight. Its trust boundary is the same one as "the panel can send console commands" and "the panel can edit .server.json": anyone who can change this config could already run things on this machine.

There are two ways to change the launch spec: select the instance and press ⚙ in the pane header, or edit .server.json directly through the file manager (changes take effect on the next start). An instance's kind cannot be changed after creation — switching kinds would turn it into a different thing, and that should not happen silently inside "save settings".

docs.title: frp tunneling
docs.text:
The frp button in the top bar opens the tunnel panel, backed by frp/frpc.toml:

  • Status: whether frpc is running and whether the binary has been downloaded
  • Connection settings: serverAddr / serverPort / auth.token, written back to frpc.toml on save
  • Start / stop: the same process the terminal menu drives
  • Download / update frpc: fetch the binary from the mirror or GitHub Releases. If the download will not go through you are not stuck: the panel shows the GitHub releases page and an Upload frpc button — download the archive yourself (or the unpacked frpc / frpc.exe) and hand it over; archives are unpacked automatically
  • Tunnel list: name, type, local address and port, remote port or domains, each removable
  • Add tunnel: tcp / udp need a remote port, http / https need domains (comma separated)

The panel only touches those keys; everything else already in frpc.toml is read and written back untouched — including other arrays-of-tables such as [[visitors]]. It shares the same read/write implementation as the terminal menu. The one exception is comments: the minimal TOML reader/writer does not preserve them, so saving once drops them.

The upload fallback sniffs the content, not the filename (browsers rename things): a zip / tar.gz gets unpacked, a bare binary is taken as-is. It does check that what comes out looks like an executable for this platform — grabbing the wrong platform's archive (say a linux tarball on Windows) is refused on the spot and the half-written file is removed, rather than installing an frpc.exe that dies with a format error on first run.

The panel manages vanilla frp. OpenFrp's cloud tunnels use a different API, and the panel only covers the small "bind it to an instance" step: fill in the user token and tunnel id under instance settings, and decide whether to raise the tunnel with the instance.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
The first run generates a random token, writes it into web.token under config.json, and prints a URL carrying it:

Web panel started: http://127.0.0.1:8765/?token=xxxxxxxx
Access token: xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

Open that once and the token lands in a cookie; after that http://127.0.0.1:8765/ is enough. Verification uses a constant-time comparison and only accepts the value of the mstl_token cookie itself.

The three ways of presenting a token (X-MSTL-Token header, mstl_token cookie, ?token= query parameter) are equally valid — matching any one of them is enough. So when the browser still holds a cookie from an older token, the correct new token in the address bar still works, and it overwrites the stale cookie on the way in.

After "regenerate access token" in the menu, a running panel accepts the new token immediately — no restart needed; the menu prints the new URL for you.

docs.title: "Access token missing or invalid"
docs.text:
Check these in order:

  1. A stale cookie is in the way. The browser may still hold a cookie from a previous token. Force-reload with Ctrl+F5, or clear this site's cookies, then open the full URL the menu printed.
  2. 127.0.0.1 vs localhost. The browser treats them as different sites, so cookies are not shared. Keep using whichever one you started with.
  3. You just regenerated the token. Use the newly printed URL; the token in the old one is dead.

The 401 page lists these same three hints.

docs.title: Security boundary
docs.text:
The panel can send commands to a server console, rewrite files inside the instance directory, and configure an instance to execute arbitrary commands — so it hands both a command channel and the instance tree to a browser. The daemon runs as your user, so one click can stop a server, change ops, edit server.properties, delete files, or point a generic instance at any command. Therefore:

  • It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, unreachable from outside the machine
  • Every /api route requires the token
  • To reach it through frp, put a reverse proxy and HTTPS in front. Do not leave the panel bare, and think twice before changing web.host
  • Holding the token means holding read/write access to the instance directory and this command channel; there is no switch that turns the file manager or generic instances off

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Field Default Description web.host "127.0.0.1" Bind address; 0.0.0.0 means all interfaces web.port 8765 Bind port; 0 means "pick a free one" web.token "" Access token; generated on first start when empty web.auto_start false Start the panel with the app. Runs on a background thread and does not block the terminal menu; toggled under the panel submenu [4]

About port 8765

8765 is also the default port of VS Code's Python debugger (debugpy). If you start the panel while debugging Python, the two compete for it; on Windows SO_REUSEADDR used to let the second bind "succeed" silently, which showed up as intermittent 401s or a panel that would not load. That option is now disabled on Windows, so the conflict is reported as a bind failure. Just pick another port.

Command-line flags can override host and port for one run:

python start.py web --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9000

docs.title: API surface
docs.text:
The entire contract between the front end and the back end:

Method Path Description GET /api/state Instance list plus a batch of UI strings in the current language GET /api/stream SSE event stream; one subscription covers every instance. Add ?name=<instance> to narrow it to one POST /api/start Body {"name": "..."} POST /api/stop Body {"name": "..."} POST /api/command Body {"name": "...", "command": "..."} GET /api/files ?name=<instance>&path=<relative> — list a folder GET /api/file ?name=&path= — read a text file GET /api/file/raw ?name=&path= — download raw bytes POST /api/file/write {"name": "...", "path": "...", "content": "..."} POST /api/file/mkdir {"name": "...", "path": "..."} POST /api/file/rename {"name": "...", "path": "...", "new_name": "..."} POST /api/file/delete {"name": "...", "path": "..."} POST /api/file/extract {"name": "...", "path": "...", "dest"?, "overwrite"?} — unpack an archive in place POST /api/file/upload ?name=&path=; the request body is the file, read to exactly Content-Length GET /api/cores Server core list; add ?type=<core> for that core's versions POST /api/instances {"name", "kind"?, "mc_version", "min_mem", "max_mem", "core_type"?, "core_version"?, "jar_name"?, "launch"?} POST /api/instances/settings Update an instance: {"name", "min_mem"?, "extra_jvm_args"?, "launch"?, "openfrp"?, "auto_start"?, ...}; kind and name are not changeable POST /api/instances/import/scan {"zip_path": "..."} — returns the candidate cores POST /api/instances/import/commit {"zip_path": "...", "jar": "...", "name": "..."} POST /api/instances/import/abort {"zip_path": "..."} — discards the extracted temp folder GET /api/frp frpc status + connection settings + tunnel list POST /api/frp/settings {"serverAddr", "serverPort", "token"} POST /api/frp/proxy Add a tunnel: {"name", "type", "localIP", "localPort", "remotePort"?\|"customDomains"?} POST /api/frp/proxy/delete {"index": 0} POST /api/frp/start Start frpc POST /api/frp/stop Stop frpc POST /api/frp/download Download / update the frpc binary

Conventions:

  • A failure always returns {"ok": false, "key": "<i18n key>", "message": "<explanation in the current language>"} with HTTP 400; an unexpected exception returns 500. The front end simply shows message
  • There are three event shapes: {"type": "line", ...} for a console line, {"type": "state", ...} for a state change, and {"type": "job", ...} for long-task progress (carrying label / ratio / done). line and state carry an instance field saying where they came from, plus a per-instance monotonic seq — on reconnect the server replays the whole history, and the front end uses seq to skip lines it has already drawn instead of duplicating them. job belongs to no instance, so it is never filtered by the per-instance subscription
  • Lines with kind: "note" are produced by MSTL itself, already translated by the server before being pushed
  • The download POSTs are synchronous and their progress rides the SSE stream above; uploads report progress straight from the browser (XMLHttpRequest.upload.onprogress), with the server uninvolved

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
This is the closed loop plus a few everyday panels, not a full operations panel. Not yet done: plugin and mod management, restoring "which servers were running" after a restart, and managing OpenFrp cloud tunnels from the panel (creating and deleting those still goes through the terminal menu).

The file manager keeps deliberate limits too: one file at a time (no multi-select or bulk delete), empty folders cannot be uploaded (the directory picker never reports them), extraction covers zip and tar only (7z / rar would need an external tool), there is no disk-usage column and no resumable transfers.

Each of those would plug into the same core/ surface.

docs.title: Guide
docs.text:
Covers the day-to-day use of MSTL in the order "install it → run it → configure it".

  • Quick start: from nothing to your first startable server
  • Server management: multiple instances, version isolation, import and export
  • Configuration: the complete field reference for global and per-server config

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: MSTL has two layers of configuration: the global config.json, and a .server.json for each instance.

docs.title: Global configuration config.json
docs.text:
It lives at the project root (next to the executable in a packaged build) and is generated from the default values when missing.

{
  "java_path": null,
  "interactive": true,
  "language": "",
  "curseforge_api_key": "",
  "download_threads": 16,
  "auto_start_server": "",
  "web": {
    "host": "127.0.0.1",
    "port": 8765,
    "token": ""
  },
  "ai": {
    "enabled": false,
    "base_url": "",
    "model": "",
    "api_key": ""
  }
}
Field Type Default Description java_path string | null null Path to a Java executable. null means auto-detect interactive bool true Whether to enter the interactive console after the server starts, i.e. type server commands straight into the terminal language string "" UI language. An empty string follows the system (Chinese environments get zh, everything else en); zh / en / ru can also be set explicitly curseforge_api_key string "" CurseForge API key. Left empty, CurseForge mod search is unavailable download_threads int 16 Number of concurrent download chunks. Falls back to a single thread when the mirror does not support Range requests auto_start_server string "" Name of the server that "Settings" has marked as the default to launch; empty means no auto-start. That one is launched in the foreground and skips the menu web.host string "127.0.0.1" Web panel bind address; 0.0.0.0 means all interfaces web.port int 8765 Web panel bind port; 0 means "pick a free one" web.token string "" Web panel access token; generated on first start when empty web.auto_start bool false Whether the panel starts with the app. It runs on a background thread and does not block the terminal menu ai.enabled bool false Whether the AI assistant tab in the web panel is enabled ai.base_url string "" OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint, e.g. https://api.openai.com/v1 ai.model string "" Model id, e.g. gpt-4o-mini ai.api_key string "" API key. The MSTL_AI_API_KEY environment variable wins over this value, and the panel never echoes a stored key

The language, download_threads, and auto_start_server fields normally do not need hand-editing; use menu [7] Settings instead:

  • [1] Language: lists the languages available under locales/, with an [A] option to go back to following the system
  • [2] Download threads: adjust the concurrency live
  • [3] Check for updates: reads the current version from version.json and compares it against the latest GitHub Release
  • [4] Auto-start server: choose which server the main menu launches by default
  • [5] Run at startup: writes the Windows registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run; unavailable on non-Windows platforms

The bind address, port, token and "start with the app" flag all live in the main menu's [8] Web panel submenu, so config.json normally needs no hand-editing. Usage and the security boundary are covered in Web panel.

Two different \"auto-start\" switches

  • auto_start_server (global, one server): the app skips the main menu and runs that instance in the foreground — the terminal belongs to it, Ctrl+C ends it.
  • An instance's auto_start (one per instance): the app raises it in the background, so the terminal stays on the menu; its console is visible in the panel, and it is stopped when the app exits.

When both point at the same instance, only the foreground path runs — it is never started twice.

About config.json and version control

config.json holds machine-specific settings, so the repository ships only config.example.json as a template. After you clone the project, config.json is generated from the defaults and is not tracked by git.

docs.title: Per-server configuration .server.json
docs.text:
It lives at servers/<server name>/.server.json.

{
  "name": "survival",
  "mc_version": "1.21.1",
  "jar": "paper.jar",
  "java_path": null,
  "min_mem": "2G",
  "max_mem": "8G",
  "extra_jvm_args": [],
  "extra_server_args": [],
  "process_priority": "normal",
  "auto_restart": false,
  "restart_max": 5,
  "openfrp": {
    "token": "",
    "proxy_id": 0,
    "auto_start": false
  }
}
Field Type Default Description name string "" Display name, used to identify the instance in menus mc_version string "" Minecraft version, used to derive the required Java version jar string "server.jar" Core jar file name, relative to the server directory java_path string | null null Overrides the global Java setting; null keeps the auto-detected result min_mem string "1G" -Xms; G / M units are supported max_mem string "4G" -Xmx extra_jvm_args list[str] [] Extra JVM arguments, such as -XX:+UseG1GC extra_server_args list[str] [] Extra server arguments, such as --nogui process_priority string "normal" Process priority: normal / below (below normal) / low kind string "minecraft" Instance kind: minecraft or generic. Cannot be changed after creation auto_start bool false Start with the app: raised in the background when the app starts, manageable from the panel auto_restart bool false Restart on crash: brought back automatically when the process exits with a non-zero code (5s backoff, doubling, capped at 60s). A manual stop, stop typed into the console, or a clean shutdown (exit code 0) never triggers it restart_max int 5 How many consecutive crashes before giving up, range 0–20; 0 disables it. Surviving 60 seconds resets the counter launch object see below The generic instance launch spec; ignored when kind is minecraft openfrp.token string "" OpenFrp user token bound to this instance openfrp.proxy_id int 0 Bound tunnel ID; 0 means unbound openfrp.auto_start bool false Whether to start frpc automatically when the server launches

A generic instance's launch block:

Field Type Default Description mode string "exec" exec (run an executable directly, no shell) / cmd / powershell program string "" With mode=exec, the executable; relative paths resolve inside the instance args list[str] [] With mode=exec, one argument per entry command string "" With mode=cmd / powershell, the command string workdir string "" Working directory, relative to the instance; empty means the instance itself

process_priority, extra_jvm_args, extra_server_args, auto_start, auto_restart (and a generic instance's whole launch block) can be changed from the configuration menu that appears after selecting an instance under main menu [1] Start server — no hand-editing needed. In the web panel, select the instance and press ⚙ in the pane header.

docs.title: Auto-generated files
docs.text:
File Description Tracked by git config.json Global configuration No java_list.json Java detection results and the last selection, to avoid a full scan every time No msl_cache.json Server types and version lists from the MSL mirror, cached per day No version.json Written by CI at packaging time, holds the version number used by the update check No

All of these are safe to delete; MSTL rebuilds them on the next run.

docs.title: Java requirements
docs.text:
MC version Minimum Java Recommended Java Notes ≤ 1.12.2 8 8 Many older mods require Java 8 1.13 – 1.16.5 8 11 Java 11 performs better 1.17 – 1.17.1 16 17 Java 8 is no longer compatible 1.18 – 1.20.4 17 17 ≥ 1.20.5 21 21 Mandated upstream ≥ 1.25 25 25 Latest snapshots

When the requirement is not met, startup prints a warning and offers an automatic JDK download (17 / 21 / 25, from GraalVM).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Item Requirement Python 3.10 or newer (needed only when running from source) Third-party packages None. Everything uses the standard library Java Optional. MSTL can download a JDK automatically when Java is missing or the version does not match

If you use a prebuilt archive from a release (the Windows MSTL.exe, or the Linux / macOS binary), you do not even need Python installed.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Run from sourceUse a packaged build 
git clone https://github.com/yzsyzdy/Minecraft-Terminal-Server-Launcher.git
cd Minecraft-Terminal-Server-Launcher
python start.py

Grab the archive for your platform from Releases — no Python required.

Windows: MSTL-v*.zip, unzip it and double-click MSTL.exe.

Linux (x86_64):

mkdir mstl && tar xzf MSTL-v*-linux-x86_64.tar.gz -C mstl
cd mstl && ./MSTL

macOS: use -macos-arm64 on Apple silicon, -macos-x86_64 on Intel.

mkdir mstl && tar xzf MSTL-v*-macos-arm64.tar.gz -C mstl
cd mstl && ./MSTL

Two limits on the non-Windows builds

  • The macOS build is not code-signed (that needs an Apple developer certificate). If Gatekeeper blocks the first launch, right-click → Open, or run xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ./MSTL.
  • The Linux build needs glibc 2.35 or newer (it is built on Ubuntu 22.04). On older distributions, use the Run from source tab above.

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
The first launch creates three things in the current directory:

config.json      # global configuration
servers/         # server instances, one subdirectory each
java_list.json   # Java detection cache (written after the first scan)

If servers/ is empty, the main menu will walk you through importing or downloading a server first.

docs.title: Option A: download a server core
docs.text:
Main menu → [3] New instance → [1] Download a Minecraft server core:

  1. Pick a server type (Paper, Purpur, Fabric, Forge, Velocity, and 30-odd more)
  2. Pick a version (the version list is cached for a day to avoid repeat requests)
  3. Confirm, and the core is downloaded with multiple threads into a new server directory
  4. Fill in the server name, memory, and other settings as prompted

docs.title: Option B: import an existing server
docs.text:
Main menu → [2] Import server archive:

  1. Enter the path to the archive
  2. MSTL unpacks it into a temporary directory and detects the core jar automatically
  3. If several jars are found, it asks you to pick one
  4. Confirm, and it lands in servers/<name>/

docs.title: Option C: create a generic instance
docs.text: Main menu → [3] New instance → [2] Generic instance. It does not run Minecraft; it runs an executable of your choosing, or a cmd / powershell command — with the same start/stop, live console and log file. See Generic instances.

docs.title: Starting
docs.text:
Main menu → [1] Start server, then pick a server. Before launching, MSTL does a few things in order:

  1. Resolve Java: cache → system scan → download if necessary
  2. Validate compatibility: compare against the Java version the MC version needs, warn and offer a download if it does not match
  3. Verify the core: make sure both the java executable and the jar exist
  4. Assemble the command: -Xms / -Xmx, extra JVM arguments, extra server arguments

After it starts you land in an interactive console. Type server commands directly (stop, say hello, op <player>, and so on); input is passed straight through to the server process.

docs.title: EULA
docs.text:
A Minecraft server exits immediately on first launch if the EULA has not been accepted. MSTL spots eula=false and asks whether you agree:

  • Agree → it rewrites eula.txt and restarts the server
  • Decline → this launch ends

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Tired of sitting at the terminal: main menu [8] Web panel — start, watch the console, manage files and frp from a browser. See Web panel
  • Want to tune memory or JVM flags: Configuration
  • Want to install plugins or mods: Plugin management, Mod management
  • Want friends to connect: Tunneling

docs.title: Directory layout
docs.text:
Every subdirectory of servers/ is one server instance, fully isolated from the others:

servers/
├── survival/
│   ├── .server.json        # configuration for this server
│   ├── paper.jar           # the core
│   ├── eula.txt
│   ├── server.properties
│   ├── plugins/            # plugins
│   ├── mods/               # mods (Fabric / Forge, etc.)
│   └── world/              # world data
└── skyblock/
    └── ...

The directory name is the instance identifier. Non-ASCII characters are fine (everything is handled as UTF-8 internally), but paths containing \ / : * ? " < > | will misbehave on Windows.

docs.title: Version isolation
docs.text:
Each instance records its own MC version, core jar, Java path, memory limit, and JVM arguments. A 1.20.1 Forge server and a 1.21.1 Paper server can coexist, each on its own Java.

At launch the required Java is derived from mc_version in .server.json, so a single MSTL.exe can serve both old and new versions.

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
Main menu → [2] Import server archive.

Behaviour details:

  • .zip is supported. Extraction goes through a temporary directory that is cleaned up afterwards, so servers/ is never polluted
  • Only jars in the top level of the archive are considered as core candidates, so jars inside plugins/ are not mistaken for cores
  • When more than one candidate exists, you pick interactively
  • If the archive already contains a .server.json, its settings are read in
  • If the archive has an extra wrapping directory (for example, a zipped folder rather than its contents), MSTL handles the nesting

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
Main menu → [5] Export server packages an existing instance by category, for migration or backup.

Available categories:

Category Contents world world, world_nether, world_the_end datapacks world/datapacks plugins plugins/*.jar plugindata plugins/*/, the data directories of each plugin playerdata Player data, statistics, advancements, ops.json, whitelist.json, ban lists, and so on icon server-icon.png config server.properties, bukkit.yml, paper.yml, purpur.yml, eula.txt, .server.json, and so on

playerdata involves player privacy, so it is unchecked by default; turn it on manually when you need it.

Once you have made your selection, MSTL collects the files by category into a zip. Note that the core jar is not part of any category (a version upgrade usually means a new core), so add it back after importing.

docs.title: Day-to-day plugin and mod handling
docs.text:
Main menu → [4] Manage plugins/mods, then pick a server:

  • Lists the jars in the directory with their enabled/disabled state
  • Enable / Disable: implemented by renaming. Disabling turns the file into .jar.disabled, which the server will not load
  • Delete: removes the file after confirmation
  • Import a local jar: copies an existing jar from disk into the folder
  • Search and download: searches the online sources and installs

See Plugin management and Mod management for details.
